units.translation: Wecklein's conjecture is (in Aeschylean Studies p. 83 and in the dissertation on ephetai and naukraroi in the Proceedings of the Bavarian Academy, historical-philological class, 1873, fasc. 1, p. 43) ναύονθ᾽ ὅμιλον τῶνδ᾽ ἀγωνίων θεῶν [a suppliant throng of these contest gods], since ὅμιλον [throng] is more fittingly said of suppliants than of gods, comparing the glosses of Hesychius ναύειν: ἱκετεύειν [to supplicate], from the fact that suppliants flee to the hearth. ναύω: λίσσομαι, ἱκετεύω [I pray, I supplicate]. And Photius' ναύειν: ἱκετεύειν [to supplicate], since they were in temples, or from the hearth, from ἐναῦσαι [to kindle]. There is no reason why ὅμιλος [throng], which is said of a crowd or assembly of men and is not infrequently used by Homer of a crowd of fighters, should be denied the ability to be said of an assembly of contest gods, just as Homer said θεῶν ὁμήγυριν [assembly of gods] and Aeschylus θεῶν πανήγυριν [gathering of gods]. Much more offensive is the placement of ὅμιλον [throng] in such a way that it must be construed by the reader with the genitives τῶνδ᾽ ἀγωνίων θεῶν [of these contest gods], not referred to other persons, which is all the more incredible to have pleased Aeschylus since it was easy to write ναύονθ᾽ ὅμιλον τούσδ᾽ ἀγωνίους θεούς [a throng supplicating these contest gods], i.e. a throng supplicating the contest gods. To this is added that the verb ναύω is so strange that it is permissible to suspect an error of the ancient glossographer: this suspicion is increased by the glosses of the grammarians which assign the same meaning of supplicating to the compounds ἐναύω, whose authenticity is certain, and ἐνάζω, which was perhaps formed from the aorist ἐναῦσαι, on which see Thes. vol. 3 p. 1063 and Schmidt on Hesychius s.v. ἐνάζω. Hesychius noted a noun derived from the verb ναύω, ναυστῆρες: οἱ ἱκέται [suppliants]. For thus Lobeck, Technol. p. 13, corrected for οἱ οἰκέται [household slaves], though hesitantly: for since vaῦλον is called τὸ ἐνοίκιον [rent] (in Pollux 1, 75 and 10, 20), it seemed consistent that vαυστῆρας were called τοὺς ἐνναέτας [inhabitants], i.e. domestic and familiar, by which name are included οἱ οἰκέται [household slaves], about which he spoke on p. 7. Below at 503, where now is read ναύτην ἄγοντας τόνδ᾽ ἐφέστιον θεῶν [bringing this sailor as a suppliant at the hearth of the gods], Wecklein wished to restore ναυστῆρ᾽, or ναυστήν, or writing ναυτήν with only the accent changed, which is all the more improbable since Aeschylus elsewhere consistently said ἱκέτην [suppliant]. In another way the grammarians erred who confused ναύειν with νάειν (to flow), as Hesychius ναύει: ῥέει, βλύζει [flows, gushes], for which below correctly νάουσι: ῥέουσι [they flow], and corruptly ναῦσι: ῥέουσι [they flow]. Another corruption (after ναυστῆρες) ναυστήρα: μεγάλην, φοβεράν [great, fearful], which Schmidt conjectured arose from αὐστηράν [harsh].
